scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: the NOC got a transient alert and now believes a core
backbone router (R6, possibly R7) "crashed and is down," and that traffic which
transits the core toward the far end of the network is being black-holed. They
want the crashed backbone router confirmed and recovered. Please confirm the fault.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The NOC alert claiming that backbone router R6 (or R7) "crashed and is down" and
that core-transit traffic is being black-holed is a false alarm. Direct inspection
of every implicated device reveals a fully healthy network.

R6 has all four physical interfaces (eth0–eth3) in the UP/UP state with correct IP
addresses (46.1.1.2/8 toward R4, 56.1.1.2/8 toward R5, 67.1.1.1/8 toward R7,
60.1.1.1/8 stub). All five FRR daemons (watchfrr, zebra, mgmtd, ospfd, staticd)
are running. R6 holds three OSPF Full adjacencies: with R4 (14.1.4.1 via eth0),
R5 (15.1.4.1 via eth1), and R7 (67.1.1.2 via eth2). Its routing table is fully
populated with OSPF-learned routes covering every prefix in the topology.

R7 similarly has both interfaces UP, all FRR daemons running, and one OSPF Full
adjacency (with R6 via eth0). R7's routing table is fully populated; its loopbacks
(17.1.x.1) are properly redistributed into OSPF and visible in R6's RIB.

End-to-end data-plane verification confirms no black-holing: pc0 → pc12 = 0%
loss; pc0 → R7 (far-end stub 70.x.x.x) = 0% loss; r9 → R8 = 0% loss; R6 →
R7 traceroute = 1 hop with no loss. R3's RIB contains valid routes to 70.0.0.0/8
(R7's segment) and 80.0.0.0/8 (R8's segment) via R4.

Root cause: There is no fault; the monitoring alert was a false positive — no
backbone router has crashed or lost adjacency, and no traffic path is impaired.

Corrective action: Acknowledge and close the ticket; investigate the monitoring
system's alerting threshold or flap-detection logic that generated the erroneous
trigger.
